kwan:
How to tie a Kwan. This simple Gulf Coast pattern could be a crab, a shrimp or a baitfish, and redfish eat it in all three moods. Dumbbell eyes make it hop along the bottom with the hook riding up.

You'll need a saltwater hook, size one to four. Tan three-oh thread. Dumbbell eyes, craft fur or a rabbit strip for the tail, chenille or dubbing for the body, and optional rubber legs.

Step one. Tie the dumbbell eyes on behind the hook eye with tight figure-eight wraps.

Step two. At the bend, tie in a tail of craft fur or a short rabbit strip.

Step three. Wind the chenille forward, around and past the eyes, adding a pair of rubber legs on each side if you like.

Step four. Tie off in front of the eyes and whip finish.

Hop it slowly in front of tailing or cruising redfish, and let it settle to the bottom.

bonefish-special:
How to tie a Bonefish Special. Chico Fernandez's classic is one of the original bonefish flies. An orange tail, a gold body and a white wing with grizzly sides make a simple, buggy shrimp for skinny water.

You'll need a saltwater hook, size four to eight. Black one-forty-denier thread. Orange marabou and pearl Krystal Flash for the tail. Gold tinsel under clear D-Rib for the body. White calf tail and grizzly hackles for the wing, and thick UV finish for the head.

Step one. At the bend, tie in an orange marabou tail with a few strands of pearl flash.

Step two. Wrap a smooth gold tinsel body, then cover it with clear D-Rib in touching turns.

Step three. At the front, tie in a wing of white calf tail with a grizzly hackle on each side.

Step four. Build a neat head and coat it with UV finish.

Fish it in skinny water with short, slow strips.

spoon-fly:
How to tie a Spoon Fly. It's the fly-rod version of a gold weedless spoon, and on a windy day with murky water, redfish find it when nothing else works. Thin layers of resin give it a domed shape that wobbles.

You'll need a curved-shank or slightly bent saltwater hook. Fine gold or tan thread. Wide gold Flashabou or mylar sheet, thick UV resin or five-minute epoxy, and twenty to twenty-five pound hard mono for a weed guard.

Step one. Lay a thread base along the whole shank, and tie in a piece of hard mono at the bend if you want a weed guard.

Step two. Lay strips of wide gold flash along the top of the shank, and tie them down at both ends to form a flat oval.

Step three. Build up thin layers of resin over the flash, curing each one, until you have a domed spoon shape.

Step four. Keep the shape even from side to side, so the fly wobbles instead of spinning.

Step five. Bring the mono up to the eye as a weed guard loop, tie it down and whip finish.

Fish it in murky water and on windy days, when redfish are rooting in the grass. Gold is the go-to color.

seaducer:
How to tie a Seaducer. Made from nothing but saddle hackles, this old saltwater pattern lands softly and hovers over shallow grass where weighted flies would snag. Snook, redfish and seatrout all love it.

You'll need a saltwater hook, size one to one-aught. Red flat-waxed nylon thread. Four to six saddle hackles with a little flash for the tail, three or four webby saddles for the body, and hard mono for an optional weed guard.

Step one. Lay a thread base to the bend. If you want a weed guard, tie in a piece of hard mono first.

Step two. Tie in two or three saddle hackles on each side, with the curves splaying outward, plus a few strands of flash.

Step three. Tie in a webby saddle hackle by its tip at the bend.

Step four. Palmer it forward in touching turns, adding new hackles as each one runs out, until you reach the eye.

Step five. Form the weed guard loop if you're using one, whip finish and cement the head.

It's great over shallow grass and potholes where weighted flies snag. Red and white, yellow and grizzly, and black are the classics.

tarpon-toad:
How to tie a Tarpon Toad. Its dense chenille head pushes water and its short tail kicks with every strip. Laid-up and rolling tarpon eat it when they won't look at anything else.

You'll need a heavy-wire tarpon hook, size two-aught. Flat-waxed nylon thread. A short rabbit strip or marabou for the tail, a few strands of Krystal Flash, large synthetic chenille like Ice or Cactus Chenille, and bead-chain or plastic eyes.

Step one. Lay a thread base along the rear half of the shank.

Step two. Tie in a short rabbit or marabou tail with a few strands of flash, about one and a half shank lengths long.

Step three. Tie in the chenille at the bend and wrap it forward densely, pulling the fibers back after each turn.

Step four. About two-thirds of the way up, tie in the eyes, and keep wrapping chenille around them with figure-eight wraps.

Step five. Tie off and whip finish, then trim the bottom of the chenille flat so the fly rides upright.

Use long, slow strips for rolling and laid-up tarpon. When one eats, strip-strike. Never lift the rod like a trout set.

partridge-and-orange:
How to tie a Partridge and Orange. This North Country spider has been catching trout in England for centuries. It's nothing but silk and a partridge feather, but the soft fibers breathe like the legs of an emerging insect.

You'll need a wet fly hook, size twelve to sixteen. Orange silk thread, a pinch of hare's fur if you want a thorax, and a grey partridge feather.

Step one. Wrap a thin, smooth silk body over the front two-thirds of the shank.

Step two. If you like, dub a tiny thorax of hare's fur just behind the eye.

Step three. Prepare a partridge feather and tie it in by the tip.

Step four. Wind just one or two turns of hackle, tie it off, and finish a small head.

Swing it across the current during a hatch, or fish it upstream in a team of spiders.

pheasant-tail-soft-hackle:
How to tie a Pheasant Tail Soft Hackle. This simple wet fly combines a pheasant tail body with a partridge collar. Swung through a riffle during a hatch, it looks just like an emerging mayfly or caddis.

You'll need a wet fly hook, size twelve to eighteen. An optional gold bead. Brown eight-oh thread. Pheasant tail fibers for the body, copper wire for the rib, peacock herl for the thorax, and a partridge feather.

Step one. Tie in the copper wire and a few pheasant tail fibers at the bend. Wrap the fibers forward as the body, then rib them with the wire.

Step two. Wrap a small thorax of peacock herl just behind the eye.

Step three. Wind one or two turns of partridge as a collar, tie it off and whip finish.

Swing it through riffles during a hatch, and let it rise at the end of the drift.

montana-nymph:
How to tie a Montana Nymph. Black and yellow chenille make this classic stonefly easy to tie and easy for trout to see. It works in rivers, and it's a favorite on stillwaters too.

You'll need a two-X-long nymph hook, size six to twelve. Black six-oh thread. Black hackle tips for the tail, black chenille for the abdomen and wing case, yellow chenille for the thorax, and a black hackle.

Step one. At the bend, tie in a short tail of black hackle tips.

Step two. Wrap a black chenille abdomen over the rear half of the shank.

Step three. Tie in a strand of black chenille for the wing case and a black hackle. Wrap a yellow chenille thorax, then palmer the hackle through it.

Step four. Pull the black chenille over the thorax, tie it down and whip finish.

Strip it or dead-drift it in rivers. It's also a top stillwater pattern.

twenty-incher:
How to tie a Twenty Incher. Mike Mercer named this stonefly nymph after the kind of trout it catches. Pheasant tail, peacock and flash make it buggy and bright at the same time.

You'll need a two-X-long nymph hook, size eight to fourteen. A gold bead. Black eight-oh thread. Brown goose biots for the tail. Pheasant tail over a peacock underbody for the abdomen, copper wire for the rib, peacock herl for the thorax, pheasant tail with flash for the wing case, and brown hen for the legs.

Step one. Slide on the bead and start the thread. At the bend, tie in two goose biots, split apart, as the tail.

Step two. Wrap the abdomen of pheasant tail over a little peacock, and rib it with the copper wire.

Step three. Tie in the wing case of pheasant tail and flash, wrap a peacock herl thorax, and tie in hen fibers on each side as legs.

Step four. Pull the wing case over the thorax, tie it down behind the bead and whip finish.

It's a searching nymph for big trout. Fish it deep through runs and pockets.

birds-nest:
How to tie a Bird's Nest. Cal Bird's scruffy nymph looks like nothing in particular and a little like everything. Its rough body and mallard legs suggest caddis pupae and mayfly nymphs.

You'll need a one-X-long nymph hook, size ten to sixteen. Tan eight-oh thread. Mallard flank fibers for the tail and legs, copper wire for the rib, and rough hare's ear or Australian opossum dubbing.

Step one. At the bend, tie in a short tail of mallard flank fibers, then the copper wire.

Step two. Dub a rough body up the shank and rib it with the wire.

Step three. Wind a few mallard flank fibers as a collar, dub over the base of the collar, and whip finish.

Dead-drift it or swing it. It suggests caddis pupae and mayfly nymphs.
